extracted.intended_audience: editors, copyeditors, authors, typesetters, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for capitalization, italics, quotations, spelling, and punctuation to be used by editors and authors preparing print or academic text. Covers when to use capitals/small caps, italics, quotation marks, spelling conventions, and detailed punctuation rules with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Scientific names in botanical/zoological/medical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological matter, the scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera; also in botanical and zoological matter, the names of species if derived from names of men or women or from generic names; but in geological and medical matter the names of species are never capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vertebrata, Reptilia, Cruciferae, Salix; Felis leo, Cocos nucijera, Rosa Carolina, Parkinsonia Torreyana, Styrax californica, Lythrum hyssopifolia, Phyleuma Halleri, Carex Halleriana. Note exception for geological usage: Pterygomatopus schmidti, Conodectus javosus.

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: The names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes should be capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Capitalize names of solar-system bodies (except common nouns)
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical work, the names of the bodies of our solar system (except 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' 'stars') should be capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. Capitalize institutional divisions, departments, officers, and courses in official university work
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University of Chicago (in all official work dealing with administration or curricula) are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the School of Education (the School), the University Extension Division (but: the division), the Department of Anthropology (but: the department), the Board of Trustees (the Trustees, the Board), the Senate, the Council, the Faculty of the College of Commerce and Administration (but: the faculty); titles: the President, the Registrar, Professor of Physics, Assistant in Chemistry, Fellow, Scholar; scholarships and course names capitalized in official contexts (but shortened common nouns may be lowercased).

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Capitals and small capitals for date line and salutatory/signature lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitals and small capitals for the names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters or articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and formatting: 'Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1910' (set to the right with one em indentation and preferably in smaller type); 'My dear Mr. Smith:' (flush, followed by a colon, same type as body, separate line unless preceded by name/address line); signature lines set to the right with one em indentation; addresses set to the left with two ems' indentation in smaller type. Address lines should be in caps and small caps and centered on the preceding line.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Use initial words like 'Whereas', 'Note', 'Section' with capitalization and punctuation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'Whereas'; in notes (not footnotes) use 'Note.' followed by a period and dash; in constitutions/by-laws use 'Section' introducing paragraphs followed by a number. The usual practice is to abbreviate 'Section' after the first occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Note.— It should be noticed that ...' ; 'Section 1. This association shall be styled ...' ; subsequent: 'Sec. 2. The object of the association, etc.'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Set a.m./p.m. and B.C./A.D. in small capitals without spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Set 'a.m.' and 'p.m.' (ante and post meridiem), and 'B.C.' and 'A.D.' in small capitals, without a space between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D. (See cross-references 22,103,106,219.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Use lower-case initial letter for words formerly proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of common usage originally proper names, and their derivatives, in whose present generalized acceptation the origin is obscured, and generally verbs derived from proper names, take a small initial letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, christianize, anglicize, macadamize.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Use lower-case for minor subdivisions in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references use lower-case for minor subdivisions and their abbreviations (chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n. (See other rules where referenced.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Abbreviate units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Units of measurement should be abbreviated in specified forms (h. = hour, min. = minute, sec. = second; lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; yd. = yard; ft. = foot; etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the listed standard abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Italic side-head capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize all but the first word and proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See examples and cross-references 172 and 280.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Capitalize first word of a quotation connected to the preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a quotation which, through a conjunction or otherwise, is immediately connected with what precedes, even if in the original the quoted word begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustration and exception in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Italicize words/phrases for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which it is desired to lend emphasis, importance, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italicize foreign words/phrases not incorporated into English and short foreign passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text and not incorporated into English; also (as a rule) single sentences or brief passages not long enough to set in reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung'; 'Napoleon's coup d'etat'; 'par excellence'; 'De gustibus non est disputandum.' Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions/places whose English meaning/position requires roman type, nor words of everyday occurrence sufficiently anglicized (list of many examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italicize titles of publications (books, plays, essays, cycles, long poems, pamphlets, treatises, periodicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of publications — books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems, and single long poems), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals should be italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Independent, the Modern Language Review, the Chicago Tribune, Report of the United States Commissioner of Education. Note: Botanical Gazette exceptions for footnotes; Books of the Bible and ancient manuscript titles set in roman (see rules 31 and 44).

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Italicize certain Latin/legal abbreviations in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words, phrases, and abbreviations used in literary and legal references such as ibid., idem, loc. cit., op. cit., ad lac, s.v., supra, infra, passim, vide, circa (ca.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize cf., i.e., e.g., v. (versus), viz., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Italicize 'See' and 'See also' in indexes/cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'See' and 'See also' when used in an index or similar compilation for cross-references may be italicized where differentiation is desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to differentiate cross-reference phrasing from context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Use roman quotation format for plaintiff/defendant names and titles with prefixes in legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of plaintiff and defendant in citations of legal causes and titles of proceedings containing prefixes like in re, ex parte, 'in the matter of' use roman type conventions shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; 'In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Formatting of address lines in speeches/reports/letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, and primary address lines in letters should be set flush, in a separate line, with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:' ; 'Mr. John Smith, 121 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.' ; 'Dear Sir: I take pleasure in announcing ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Signature title formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title added after the name: if one word, run into same line; if more than one but not longer than the name, center first letter under the name line and indent one em on the right; if longer than the name, center the name over the second line and set the title flush. Rules subject to special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary' ; 'Yours very truly,' ; 'Carter H. Harrison, Mayor of Chicago' ; 'Charles M. Gayley, Professor of English Language and Literature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Use of a), b), c) for subdivisions and suffix letters for fractional parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c), etc., to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double parentheses if run in); and a, b, c, etc., affixed to verse/page numbers to denote fractional parts (e.g., Luke 4:3ra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting conventions for subdividing text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Use letters for unknown quantities and similar in technical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters used to designate unknown quantities, lines, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter should be used (e.g., ac+bc=c(a+b); lines a and b; the nth power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of algebraic notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Use letters in legends and text referring to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters in legends or in the text referring to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).'

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. References to particular letters formatted plainly
rubrics_metrics.description: References to particular letters should be set plainly: the letter u, a small v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: 70. Place currency/shilling abbreviations after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 5s. and 6d. (s. and d. = shillings and pence) following numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 35s. 6d.

rubrics_metrics.name: 71. Italicize scientific names of genera/species when used together and astronomical names
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, botanical, and geological matter, scientific (Latin) names of genera and species when used together, and in astronomical matter, names of stars or constellations, should be italicized. Note: in medical matter common practice is to print such names in roman avoiding italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Conodectes favosus, Saturn, Cassiopeia. (See rules 46 and 48.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 72. Use 'Resolved.' in resolutions and capitalize it
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions the word 'Resolved.' should be used and capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 39 for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 73. Use 'Continued' after headlines/titles and 'To be continued' at end of articles
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, as a rule, use the word 'Continued;' and 'To be continued' at the end of articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY — Continued' ; note bracketed form '[To be continued]'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 74. Use quotation marks for citations run into the text
rubrics_metrics.description: Put between quotation marks (roman type) citations run into the text of a passage from an author in his own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 85 for length and reduced type rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 75. Use quotation marks for consecutive quotations from different authors or works
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from different authors, or from different works by the same author, following each other uninterrupted by intervening original matter or references, even though reduced, should be set between quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 85-87 for reduced type rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 76. Quotation marks for word-definition pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks when a word or phrase is accompanied by its definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Drop-folio' means a page-number at the foot of the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: 77. Quotation marks for unusual/technical/ironical words or phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for an unusual, technical, ironical, etc., word or phrase in the text, whether or not accompanied by an explanatory word like 'so-called.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; she wore a gown of 'lobster-colored' silk; He was elected 'master of the rolls'; 'man of affairs' used in quotes; the so-called 'man of affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 78. Use quotation marks for translations
rubrics_metrics.description: In translations, put the English equivalent of a foreign word, phrase, or passage in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Mommsen Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: 79. Use quotation marks to direct attention to particular words/phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for the particular word or words to which attention is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'; the name 'Chicago.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 80. Quotation marks for serial titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for serial titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters' series; 'International Critical Commentary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 81. Quotation marks for titles of shorter poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of shorter poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.' (See rule 60 re distinctions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 82. Quotation marks for titles of subdivisions and short works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters) of publications; titles of papers, lectures, sermons, articles, toasts, mottoes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I, 'The British School,' chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; articles 'Cross', 'Crucifixion' in Hastings' Dictionary of the Bible; lectures and toasts examples. Note Botanical Gazette exception for footnotes. References to Preface/Introduction/Table of Contents/Index should be set with capitals without quotation marks when referring to those sections (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: 83. Quotation marks for names of ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for names of ships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 84. Quotation marks for titles of works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 85. Set long quotations in smaller type (reduced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily set all prose extracts that will make five or more lines in smaller type, and poetry citations of two lines or more, in reduced type; isolated short prose quotations may be run into text if organically related; short lines adjacent to longer reduced extracts may be reduced for uniform appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and exception rules; see rule 86 for point-size reductions. Reduced extracts normally omit quotation marks (see 87).

rubrics_metrics.name: 86. Point-size guidance for reducing quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, reduce from 11-pt and 10-pt to 9-pt, from 9-pt to 8-pt, from 8-pt to 6-pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to rule 252 for additional detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: 87. Reduced citations should not have quotation marks (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations should generally not have quotation marks, except in cases noted (e.g., rule 75); quotation marks generally not used with italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 75 and 85-86 for exceptions and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 88. Quotation marks should include ellipses and 'etc.' when they indicate omitted matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when omission would otherwise be unclear; perfect clearness in each individual case is the best criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given showing when 'etc.' is inside vs outside quotes depending on whether it stands for omitted material of the quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 89. Repeat quotation marks at beginning of each paragraph of broken quoted prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted prose matter broken into paragraphs should have quotation marks repeated at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting rule for multi-paragraph quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90. Clearance/alignment of quotation marks when alignment desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Where alignment is desired, quotation marks should be 'cleared' — i.e., should project beyond the line of alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration provided of cleared quotation marks projecting beyond aligned text.

rubrics_metrics.name: 91. Use double quotation marks for primary quotations and single for quotations within quotations (alternating thereafter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used for primary quotations; for a quotation within a quotation use single marks; alternate back and forth for subsequent nested quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example demonstrating alternating quotation marks deep nesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 92. Spell out civil and military titles and forms of address preceding a name (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: All civil and military titles and forms of address preceding the name should be spelled out, except Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon.; abbreviate Esq. following a name. Note certain foreign abbreviations and that Rev. and Hon. are not used except in quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and exceptions listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: 93. Spell out Christian/first names in ordinary text
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian names like George, Charles, John should be spelled out (not Geo., Chas., Jno.), except where abbreviated forms are used in quoted matter or original signatures; 'von' as part of a name kept (see rule 239).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting preference for given names.

rubrics_metrics.name: 94. Spell out numbers less than three digits in ordinary reading matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading matter, spell out all numbers of less than three digits unless statistical/technical or in long groups of six or more following each other; treat per cent as figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' ; but use figures for 128 or technical enumerations. If the largest in a connected group has three or more digits, use figures for all. 'per cent' should take figures (e.g., 10 per cent).

rubrics_metrics.name: 95. Spell out round numbers (approximate figures in even units)
rubrics_metrics.description: Round numbers should be spelled out (e.g., 'five hundred') unless a more specific figure is intended (e.g., '550'); write 'fifteen hundred' over 'one thousand five hundred' in some usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating when to spell out and when to use figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 96. Spell out numbers commencing a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers commencing a sentence in ordinary reading matter should be spelled out regardless of size; if impracticable, reconstruct the sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women...' or reconstruct to avoid starting with figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: 97. Spell out sums of money occurring isolated in ordinary reading matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated cases in ordinary text should be spelled out ('two dollars'); when several such numbers occur close together or in statistical text, use figures and currency symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Admission was two dollars.' vs 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 98. Spell out time of day in ordinary reading matter; use figures in statistical/enumerative contexts and with A.M./P.M.
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day in ordinary reading matter: 'at four', 'at half-past two in the afternoon', 'at seven o'clock.' In statistical/enumerative contexts and with A.M./P.M., use figures (e.g., 4:15 P.M.), and omit 'o'clock' in such connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting distinctions for narrative vs statistical usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 99. Spell out ages in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out ages in ordinary text: 'eighty years and four months old'; 'children between six and fourteen.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format preference for ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: 100. Spell out numbers of centuries, dynasties, sessions, regiments, political divisions, thoroughfares (unless brevity needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares, and similar cases should be spelled out unless brevity is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session; Fifth Avenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101. References to particular decades in lower-case
rubrics_metrics.description: References to particular decades should be in the nineties, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the nineties.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102. Names of months spelled out except in statistical matters/long enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of months should be spelled out except in statistical matter or long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from January 1 to April 15' (omit st, nd, th after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: 103. Use 'United States' spelled out except in certain contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'United States' spelled out except in quotations and connections like General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S. SS. 'Oregon'; in footnotes and similar references use 'U.S.' or other abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references to rules 22, 52, 106.

rubrics_metrics.name: 104. Spell out 'Railroad (-way)', 'Fort', 'Mount' in geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use full words in geographical appellations: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad (not R.R. or Ry.); Fort Wayne; Mount Elias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for full forms in most cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: 105. Generally spell out names of publications but allow exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, spell out names of publications. Rule is open to modification for special instances; consider expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author's preference. Generally, when in doubt, spell out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good taste permits spelling out more readily than abbreviating.

rubrics_metrics.name: 106. Abbreviate state names following town names in addresses (specified abbreviations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In addresses with town names, use specified abbreviations for states, territories, and possessions, without space between letters (list provided: Ala., Ariz., Cal., etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See list in the text; follow cross-references for spacing and style (22, 52, 103).

rubrics_metrics.name: 107. Abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use ampersand in technical/bibliographic matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies) abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers', and use '&' in names of commercial firms (e.g., The Macmillan Co.; Macmillan & Co.; Harper Bros.; Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad). In non-technical running text, 'Company' and 'Brothers' may be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples showing both bibliographic/technical and text usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 108. Abbreviate 'Saint' before a name as 'St.' in place names but omit before apostles/church fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' before a place name (St. Louis, St. Peter's Church), but preferably omit 'St.' when referring to apostles, evangelists, and church fathers (Luke, Paul, Augustine rather than St. Luke etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting guidance and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 109. Standard abbreviations for books of the Bible in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use provided standard abbreviations for books of the Old Testament, New Testament, and Apocrypha in references to Scripture passages (Gen., Exod., Ps., Matt., Mark, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive list for accurate citation formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 110. Abbreviate volume/number/chapter/article/section/page/column/verse/line/note in bibliographic references
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical matter abbreviate words like 'volume,' 'number,' 'chapter,' 'article,' 'section,' 'page,' 'column,' 'verse,' 'line,' 'note' followed by their number (Vol., No., chap., art., sec., p., col., vs., l., n.); use pp., pp. f., pp. ff., Fig. formats as specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples with plural forms and notation for ranges and following pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: 111. Use metric and common measurement symbols after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use metric system designations and common measurement symbols following numerals (1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; cm. = cubic meter?, c.c., c.mm.; gm. = gram; gr. = grain; h. = hour, min. = minute; lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; yd., ft., in. etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specified symbols when following numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: 112. In extracts, use office style for modern authors; follow originals for older/essential cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ only slightly, use office style; in citations from Old English works or where essential to be faithful to the original, follow the original copy. Titles should always be accurately quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply judgment based on fidelity required by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 113. Form possessives of proper names ending in sibilants with apostrophe rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive of proper names ending in s or another sibilant: if monosyllabic add apostrophe + s; if more than one syllable add apostrophe alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations, Berlioz' compositions; convenience' sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: 114. Use 'a' before sounded h, long u, and the word 'one'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sounded h, long u, and the word 'one' use 'a' as the indefinite article (a hotel, a harmonic, a historical, a union, such a one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciation-based article usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 115. Do not use ligatures 'cb' and 'ce' in Latin quotations and derivatives; separate letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use ligature 'œ' and similar when quoting Latin or anglicized derivatives from Latin/Greek through Latin — separate the letters; but in Old English and modern French/other languages it is incorrect to separate certain letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Aurea prima sata est...' ; 'the Aeneid, Oedipus Tyrannus, Caesar, aesthetic, subpoena.' Versus Euvres de Balzac, chef-d'oeuvre in French.

rubrics_metrics.name: 116. Differentiate 'farther' and 'further' by meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' for 'more remote' or physical distance; use 'further' for 'moreover' or 'in addition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: 117. Use 'O' without comma in vocatives; 'Oh,' with comma for exclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative) use 'O' without a comma following; for an exclamation use 'Oh,' followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!' vs 'Oh, why did not Cerberus drag me back to hell?'

rubrics_metrics.name: 118. Retain or omit final 'e' in participles according to listed forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles ending with a syllable beginning with a vowel retain the final e in the primary word (agreeing, dyeing, eyeing, etc.); others omit the e before -ing (acknowledging, grudging, trudging, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists provided for which verbs retain or omit final e when forming participles.

rubrics_metrics.name: 119. Standard spelling list of selected words
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide standardized spellings for a large list of words; follow these preferred spellings (abridgment, acknowledgment, accouter, etc.). Make one word of 'anyone,' 'someone,' 'today,' 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'cannot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive example list of standardized American spellings and notes about University of Chicago official variants (e.g., 'comptroller').

rubrics_metrics.name: 120. Differentiate -ise and -ize endings; provide lists for -ize and -ise usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate which verbs are to be spelled with -ise vs -ize; provide lists of verbs to use -ize and -ise endings respectively (e.g., advertise, comprise, exercise with -ise; aggrandize, analyze, authorize with -ize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive lists showing correct -ize vs -ise usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: 121. Punctuation marks should be in same style/font as preceding word/letter
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'With the cry of Banzai! the regiment stormed the hill'; Luke 4:16a; No. 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: 122. Use period to end a complete sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 125 for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 123. Put period after abbreviations except where mechanically omitted; treat metric symbols as abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations, except where mechanical necessity compels omission of letters in middle of a word for which no recognized abbreviated form exists (indicated by apostrophe). Treat metric symbols as abbreviations and use a period; do not use periods after chemical symbols, 'per cent', or book formats (4to, 8vo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. 1, Chas.; 10 mm.; exceptions noted for some journals and for recognized abbreviations like IE (= Indo-European), OE, etc. Botanical and journal-specific exceptions also described.

rubrics_metrics.name: 124. Omit period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals even when they have ordinal value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: 125. Omit period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads, cut-in heads, box-heads, superscriptions, date lines, and signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, and after superscriptions and legends which are not complete sentences; also after date lines at top of communications and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to rule 50 for date lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: 126. Place period inside quotation marks; period inside parentheses if enclosed matter is independent sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods are placed inside quotation marks; placed inside parentheses when enclosed matter is an independent sentence and forms no part of preceding sentence; otherwise outside parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tennyson's 'In Memoriam.' Put the period inside the quotation marks. (This is a rule without exception.) When parentheses form part of preceding sentence, put the period outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: 127. Use exclamation point for outcry or emphatic/ironical utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point marks an outcry or an emphatic or ironical utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Long live the king!' 'Heaven forbid!' 'How funny this seems!' ; illustrative example with dramatic punctuation use.

rubrics_metrics.name: 128. Place exclamation point inside quotation marks when part of quotation, otherwise outside
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the exclamation point inside quotation marks when it is part of the quotation; otherwise place it outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations in rule 127.

rubrics_metrics.name: 129. Use interrogation point for queries or to express doubt; not for indirect questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interrogation point to mark a query or express doubt. Do not follow indirect questions with an interrogation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Who is this?' ; indirect: He asked whether he was ill. Parenthetical uncertain attributions may use '(?)' as in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 130. Place interrogation point inside quotation marks only when part of the quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point should be placed inside quotation marks only when it is a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The question: 'Who is who, and what is what?' Were you ever in 'Tsintsinnati'?

rubrics_metrics.name: 131. Use colon to mark a grammatical discontinuity greater than semicolon and less than period
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon marks a discontinuity of grammatical construction greater than that indicated by the semicolon and less than that indicated by the period; commonly used to emphasize close connection between clauses, introduce lists, or in other customary uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further sub-uses and examples are continued in subsequent rules (text cuts off here).
